 The Markets Are on a Yo-Yo. You Don’t Have to Be.
 Feeling a bit wobbly? Here are four things to consider that might provide some peace of mind.
 Listen · 5:27 min Share full article 
 Credit... Karsten Moran for The New York Times By Ron Lieber 
 Ron Lieber is in Year 19 and counting of urging calm when things seem crazy.
 Nov. 6, 2026 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda. Add The New York Times as a preferred source on Google Agrega The New York Times como fuente preferida en Google › 
 Market go down. Market go up.
 We’ve seen this kind of two-day volatility before, dozens or maybe hundreds of times for the gray-haired among us. But this go-round does feel a bit different in the wake of a political earthquake .
 And that’s fine. Markets are indeed about the feels — what humans or the trading robots they have programmed believe will happen to companies next. And big surprises that augur unpredictable change fire circuits in the brain.
 So by all means, do something. But that something isn’t necessarily buying or selling stocks. Instead, remind yourself that you are a person of above-average reserve and emotional intelligence as you consider the following points.
 Unpredictability can compound when politics cause stocks to gyrate.
 It’s nearly impossible to consistently predict how individual stocks or the overall market will perform in the short or medium term. That’s why so many people invest in index funds, dropping bits of money in at regular intervals and leaving it there for decades.
 For those who don’t invest that way, ask yourself this: Is this the moment to see whether you are some kind of market seer? Did you predict that President Trump would win in 2016? Win again in 2024? Does the “gridlock is good for the markets” thesis going around this week make sense to you — or actually defy logic? And do any of us have any earthly idea how Mr. Trump might behave now, if we ever did?
 It’s hard to forecast markets. It’s difficult to game out politics. Put the two together, and it’s an advertisement for ceasing any guesswork, holding all stocks and keeping them for the long term, come what may.
